heading: Cold open
narration: In 1960, Jacques Piccard reported a flatfish where fish appear unable to survive.

heading: Cold open
narration: Life reaches the very bottom of the Mariana Trench, nearly 11,000 metres down, where the floor is worked by scavenging amphipods, sea cucumbers, giant single-celled xenophyophores and dense microbial communities.

heading: Cold open
narration: Fish stop a few kilometres higher, held back, it seems, by the chemistry of their own cells.

heading: Cold open
narration: Most of what we know comes from baited landers that sat on the seabed in the dark and waited.

heading: Cold open
narration: They show what came to the bait, not a census of the floor.

heading: Title card
narration: What lives in the Mariana Trench?

heading: The deepest floor belongs to crustaceans
narration: Start with the vocabulary, because the trench has its own. NOAA divides the ocean into zones by depth, and the deepest of them is the hadal zone, the ocean deeper than 6,000 metres.

heading: The deepest floor belongs to crustaceans
narration: It is found almost entirely in trenches, which are long cracks where one tectonic plate dives beneath another.

heading: The deepest floor belongs to crustaceans
narration: The Mariana Trench is the deepest of these. It lies in the western Pacific, and everything in this episode lives inside that hadal band or near its upper edge.

heading: The deepest floor belongs to crustaceans
narration: The animals you would meet first at the bottom are amphipods. They are scavenging crustaceans, not shrimp, though at first glance they look a little like pale, curled shrimp.

heading: The deepest floor belongs to crustaceans
narration: In the trench they gather in swarms around anything edible that reaches the floor.

heading: The deepest floor belongs to crustaceans
narration: Some hadal species grow far larger than the amphipods you might find under seaweed on a beach.

heading: The deepest floor belongs to crustaceans
narration: One of them, Hirondellea gigas, has been collected from the Challenger Deep itself, the deepest known point of the trench.

heading: The deepest floor belongs to crustaceans
narration: Amphipods are the reason we can say with confidence that animal life reaches the very bottom. They have been caught there repeatedly and brought to the surface.

heading: The deepest floor belongs to crustaceans
narration: They live under more than 1,000 times the pressure at the surface, a figure NOAA uses to describe the trench floor.

heading: The deepest floor belongs to crustaceans
narration: That number sounds as if it should crush anything soft. It does not, and the reason matters for the rest of this story.

heading: The deepest floor belongs to crustaceans
narration: For an animal whose body is mostly water, pressure is not mainly a crushing force, because water barely compresses.

heading: The deepest floor belongs to crustaceans
narration: The damage pressure does is subtler. It distorts proteins and cell membranes, the molecular machinery that has to fold and flex in order to work.

heading: The deepest floor belongs to crustaceans
narration: Life at the bottom of the trench is a problem of chemistry, not of armour.

heading: Almost nobody has seen it; machines have waited
narration: Here is how most of this is known. Very few people have ever been to the bottom of the Mariana Trench, and a crewed dive covers a tiny patch of seabed for a few hours.

args.title: How a lander sees the floor

heading: Almost nobody has seen it; machines have waited
narration: The workhorse is the lander, an unpowered frame dropped from a ship.

heading: Almost nobody has seen it; machines have waited
narration: It carries bait, a camera, and often a trap. It falls freely to the floor, sits there, and records what came to the bait.

args.title: How a lander sees the floor

heading: Almost nobody has seen it; machines have waited
narration: Then it releases its ballast weights and floats back up. The haul is hours of footage, a trap of animals, and sometimes a water sample.

heading: Almost nobody has seen it; machines have waited
narration: That is the raw evidence behind most of the species lists you will read.

args.title: How a lander sees the floor

heading: Almost nobody has seen it; machines have waited
narration: Be clear about what that method can and cannot show. A baited camera is excellent at revealing what came to the bait: scavengers with a good sense of smell that can swim or crawl toward it.

heading: Almost nobody has seen it; machines have waited
narration: It is poor at revealing what avoided the bait, or what was never interested in it, such as animals that filter food from the water or graze the sediment.

heading: Almost nobody has seen it; machines have waited
narration: A swarm around a carcass also tells you very little about how many live there across the whole floor.

heading: Almost nobody has seen it; machines have waited
narration: So the trench's best-known residents are partly a portrait of who answers a dinner bell.

heading: Fish live in the trench, but stop short of the floor
narration: Fish are the clearest case of a limit. The Mariana Trench does have fish.

heading: Fish live in the trench, but stop short of the floor
narration: The best known is the Mariana snailfish, a small, pale, almost translucent animal with a soft, gelatinous body.

heading: Fish live in the trench, but stop short of the floor
narration: It has been filmed and collected in the trench's upper hadal reaches.

heading: Fish live in the trench, but stop short of the floor
narration: Snailfish are the dominant fish at these depths in trenches around the Pacific.

heading: Fish live in the trench, but stop short of the floor
narration: They are not the eel-like monsters of deep-sea illustration. They look more like a tadpole made of frosted glass, and on camera they drift toward bait with a slow, unhurried flutter.

heading: Fish live in the trench, but stop short of the floor
narration: No fish has been recorded anywhere near the trench's deepest floor, though, and there is a chemical explanation for why.

heading: Fish live in the trench, but stop short of the floor
narration: Many deep-sea fish carry a molecule in their tissues called TMAO, which helps proteins hold their shape under pressure.

heading: Fish live in the trench, but stop short of the floor
narration: Researchers who sampled fish from progressively deeper water found that its concentration rises with depth.

heading: Fish live in the trench, but stop short of the floor
narration: That trend cannot continue forever. Past a certain point, the dissolved molecules inside the fish would outnumber those in the surrounding seawater, and water would flow into its tissues faster than it could cope.

heading: Fish live in the trench, but stop short of the floor
narration: Extend the trend downward and it predicts a limit above the floor of the deepest trenches, a few kilometres short of the bottom. The deepest fish ever filmed sit close to that predicted line.

heading: Fish live in the trench, but stop short of the floor
narration: Notice the shape of that argument. It is a prediction that fits the observations, not a proven law.

includes: a prediction that fits the observations

heading: Fish live in the trench, but stop short of the floor
narration: It rests on a trend measured in a limited number of species, extended beyond the depths where it was measured, and then checked against where fish have actually been seen.

heading: Fish live in the trench, but stop short of the floor
narration: So far the check has held. Years of landers dropped into the deepest trenches have filmed amphipods at the bottom and no fish.

includes: a prediction that fits the observations

heading: Fish live in the trench, but stop short of the floor
narration: A lack of sightings is weaker evidence than a sighting. Still, many drops that all come back the same way add up to something you can lean on.

heading: Some of the largest single cells on Earth live there
narration: Lower than the fish, there is life of a stranger kind. Xenophyophores are giant single-celled organisms, relatives of the shelled amoebae known as foraminifera.

heading: Some of the largest single cells on Earth live there
narration: A single xenophyophore can grow to the size of your palm or larger, building a fragile, sponge-like case out of sediment grains and debris.

heading: Some of the largest single cells on Earth live there
narration: It is one cell, not an animal. In 2011, an expedition led by researchers from Scripps, working with National Geographic, used free-falling cameras to film xenophyophores deep in the Mariana Trench, below the depths where they had previously been recorded.

heading: Some of the largest single cells on Earth live there
narration: Xenophyophores matter beyond their oddness. Their cases trap particles, and other small organisms live in and around them.

heading: Some of the largest single cells on Earth live there
narration: On parts of the deep seafloor they add structure to an otherwise flat, soft landscape.

heading: Some of the largest single cells on Earth live there
narration: Whether they play that same role at the deepest points of the trench is not well established.

heading: Some of the largest single cells on Earth live there
narration: They have been seen there, but they have not been studied there the way a reef is studied.

heading: The trench lives on what falls into it
narration: No sunlight reaches the trench. Light fades fast with depth, the reds first and the blues last, and long before the hadal zone there is nothing left for photosynthesis.

heading: The trench lives on what falls into it
narration: Nothing at the bottom can grow its food from sunlight. Almost everything the trench eats arrives from above.

heading: The trench lives on what falls into it
narration: Most of it is a slow drift of dead plankton, faecal pellets and organic debris that oceanographers call marine snow.

heading: The trench lives on what falls into it
narration: Occasionally there is a larger windfall, such as a dead fish sinking from shallower water.

heading: The trench lives on what falls into it
narration: The trench's shape changes what reaches the floor. A trench is a long, steep-sided valley.

heading: The trench lives on what falls into it
narration: Material that settles on the trench walls does not stay put, because sediment slides carry it downslope, and the axis of the trench gathers organic matter from a much wider area than the patch of sea directly above it.

heading: The trench lives on what falls into it
narration: Researchers have measured how quickly microbes in Challenger Deep sediment use oxygen.

heading: The trench lives on what falls into it
narration: They found more activity than on the shallower abyssal plain nearby. The simplest reading is that the trench works as a funnel, so food collects at the bottom.

heading: The trench lives on what falls into it
narration: That is why the microbes may be the trench's most important residents, even though they are the least visible.

heading: The trench lives on what falls into it
narration: Bacteria and archaea live throughout the sediment, breaking down what falls, and everything else depends on their work.

heading: The trench lives on what falls into it
narration: You will never see them on a lander's camera. They are known from sediment cores and water samples, which are read in the laboratory through their genes and their chemistry.

heading: The trench lives on what falls into it
narration: Not everything at the bottom chases bait. Sea cucumbers, soft-bodied relatives of starfish, plough slowly across the sediment, swallowing it and digesting the organic matter it holds.

heading: The trench lives on what falls into it
narration: They are among the commonest large animals on soft deep-sea floors, and cameras have recorded them deep in the Mariana Trench.

heading: The trench lives on what falls into it
narration: Because they feed on sediment rather than carcasses, they are exactly the kind of animal a baited trap tends to miss.

heading: The trench lives on what falls into it
narration: That is a reminder that the trench's species list is shaped by the tools used to compile it.

heading: The first sighting is still argued over
narration: People have reached the floor too, and their reports are part of the record, with all the strengths and weaknesses of eyewitness evidence.

heading: The first sighting is still argued over
narration: In 1960, Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh descended into the Challenger Deep in the bathyscaphe Trieste.

heading: The first sighting is still argued over
narration: Piccard later described seeing a flatfish on the bottom. In 2012, James Cameron made a solo dive to the Challenger Deep in a purpose-built submersible, in a project supported by National Geographic.

heading: The first sighting is still argued over
narration: He described a pale, featureless floor with small amphipods moving across it.

heading: The first sighting is still argued over
narration: The flatfish is this episode's best lesson in weighing evidence. It was an eyewitness account from a trained observer, made under enormous strain, through a small window, in poor light.

heading: The first sighting is still argued over
narration: There is no photograph. It also conflicts with everything since: the chemical argument for a fish depth limit, and years of camera drops that have never shown a fish at that depth.

heading: The first sighting is still argued over
narration: Most deep-sea biologists now think Piccard saw something else, perhaps a sea cucumber, though we cannot know for certain what was really seen.

heading: The first sighting is still argued over
narration: The report is not dismissed because it is inconvenient. It is outweighed.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: This evidence establishes that life reaches the bottom of the Mariana Trench, and it names some of what lives there.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: It does not provide a full species list. The trench is long, and only a small fraction of its floor has ever been sampled or filmed.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: Landers favour scavengers. Many specimens collected from hadal depths are still waiting to be formally described.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: Microbial diversity is known mainly through genetic surveys, which detect far more than has been named.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: The evidence also does not tell us how many animals live there, how long they live, or how stable these communities are over time.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: What we have is a sketch drawn through a handful of windows, not a census.

heading: Closing
narration: At the bottom of the deepest trench, in total darkness and under more than 1,000 times the pressure at the surface, small crustaceans gather at a fallen meal.

heading: Closing
narration: A single cell builds its fragile house from mud. Microbes work through what drifts down from the sunlit sea far above.

heading: Closing
narration: The trench is not empty. It is simply very hard to see.
